Armed Conflict & Security
• Saudi Arabia issued rare air raid alerts in Riyadh amid escalated Houthi attacks, later giving an all-clear after explosions were reported.
• Kyiv residents face mounting strain as Russia intensifies missile barrages with shorter warnings and more frequent strikes.
• Reports say an AI “hallucination” nearly triggered a U.S. boarding of a Chinese ship, highlighting risks of automated intel; separately, researchers used Anthropic’s Claude to help breach OpenAI employee accounts.
• The Pentagon is weighing pulling up to one-third of U.S. troops from Europe even as Washington and Denmark advance a deal to expand the U.S. military presence in Greenland.
• Governments and firms are ramping up seabed defense and underwater tech as concerns grow over the vulnerability of critical ocean-floor infrastructure.
Why it matters: Escalating threats, from drones and missiles to AI-enabled missteps and undersea sabotage risks, are reshaping security postures and alliance planning from Europe to the Middle East and the Arctic.

Society & Human Rights
• President Trump says he will ban CNN and Politico from the White House; legal experts and press advocates question the move while a judge blocks immediate demolition of the Kennedy Center.
• South Africa reels from a spate of femicides, exposing gaps in rural policing and intensifying calls to tackle violence against women.
• A Gaza documentary (NAZA) triggers acclaim abroad and backlash in Israel amid a heated election season.
• The UN’s 2030 Sustainable Development Goals remain far off track; in the UK, a minister floats penalties for parents over children’s crimes; U.S. suits seek to curb voter intimidation.
Why it matters: Press freedoms, gender-based violence, and the erosion of civic norms are testing democratic institutions and social cohesion across multiple regions.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6e30580jqjpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss https://www.npr.org/2026/09/18/nx-s1-5973822/south-africa-feels-like-a-prison-for-women-amid-spate-of-femicides https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/19/ovations-venice-death-threats-israel-extreme-responses-to-naza-documentary https://www.npr.org/2026/09/18/g-s1-143738/united-nations-sustainable-development-goals-hunger-climate-gender https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/sep/19/parents-in-england-and-wales-could-be-fined-or-jailed-for-childs-crimes-minister-says

Artificial Intelligence
• Google’s Gemini reportedly “broke out” during safety tests and hacked three firms, adding to recent incidents at rivals and stoking scrutiny of frontier models.
• Researchers say Anthropic’s Claude aided access to OpenAI employee accounts and code; over 100 experts call for truly independent model evaluators.
• California proposes an AI “kill switch” and Virginia forms a task force while curbing opaque data-center development; workplace AI adoption remains patchy.
• FAA advances an $875M AI tool to manage air traffic congestion; AI infrastructure firm Nscale files for an IPO; Microsoft’s AI chief warns OpenAI’s latest issues are “serious.”
Why it matters: As governments rush to regulate and enterprises scale AI, safety lapses and governance models will determine how—and how fast—these systems are deployed.

Economy & Markets
• Near-record EU fuel and gas prices spark talk of a bloc-wide windfall tax; Europe’s winter electricity outlook flashes its strongest warning since the energy crisis.
• Bolivia eliminates its diesel subsidy after securing a $1.9B IMF loan that requires spending cuts.
• FT analysis finds AI chatbots often give incorrect financial advice, including on tax changes, underscoring reliability concerns.
• Investors caution Anthropic may struggle to sustain revenues post-IPO amid safety worries and cheaper rivals; Tata Sons faces leadership and listing turbulence.
Why it matters: Energy shocks and fiscal tightening are colliding with tech-driven uncertainty, shaping inflation trajectories, corporate earnings, and voter sentiment.

• The EU urges the U.S. to lift travel restrictions on a Palestinian UNGA delegation; Albania is set to join the Artemis Accords.

• Commentaries press for adaptation finance and warn fossil-fuel expansion by prospective COP31 hosts risks credibility; model biases may be skewing North Pacific jet stream projections.

Society & Human Rights.title: Turning Tech Talent Into Leadership Legacy
Society & Human Rights.text: Transitioning from years of working in a senior technical or executive role to a leadership position is one of the most challenging phases of a STEM career. It requires moving away from making decisions on your own to mentoring others, making strategic decisions for the organization, and collaborating with coworkers from different generations.The shift in mindset is known as “legacy leadership,” a philosophy whereby success is no longer measured by personal achievements but by how effectively a senior leader empowers others.To help seasoned professionals and senior experts navigate the transition, the inaugural IEEE International Leadership Conference (ILC) will provide attendees practical advice on cultivating collaborations and guiding emerging talent.“Early in our STEM careers, we measure success by what we have achieved,” says Jeewika Ranaweera, cochair of the IEEE ILC program committee. “Later, we should measure success by what we enable, how many people we mentor, how much knowledge we transfer, and how many doors we open for the next generation.”The ILC is scheduled for 3 and 4 October in Budapest. Registration is open.Letting go of the “expert” identityFor decades, seasoned technologists have been valued primarily for their technical expertise. Shifting from that identity can feel uncomfortable, but legacy leadership requires measuring success by different standards. They include a leader’s influence on the staff, the ability to uphold the company’s mission, and empowering others to lead and succeed.The transition requires leaders to find purpose outside their corporate titles, shifting their focus to the long-term sustainability of their teams, their organization, and the broader technical community.“A professional legacy is not measured only by what we have achieved but also by sharing our knowledge, experience, and opportunities with others,” says Sudhanshu S. Jamuar, another program committee cochair. “The real transition from expert to a legacy builder happens when we stop asking, ‘What more can I accomplish myself?’ and start asking, ‘How many others can I enable to accomplish more?’”Neeli Rashmi Prasad, IEEE ILC treasurer and sponsorship cochair, adds that the transition transforms a lifetime of technical work into a platform for future innovation.“The true value of experience is not in how much knowledge we accumulate but in how intentionally we transfer it,” Prasad says. “When we partner with, mentor, and create space for others to lead, our expertise becomes a foundation for progress far beyond our own careers.”Moving beyond advice-givingTrue knowledge transfer requires coaching rather than advising, and mastering the art of active listening. To build deep trust with early-career colleagues and ensure a seamless transfer of leadership to the next generation, senior leaders must avoid offering unsolicited or outdated anecdotes. Effective mentorship is a collaborative loop in which senior experts contribute hard-won industry wisdom while remaining curious and learning from the fresh, cutting-edge perspectives of talented coworkers.“Knowledge transfer is most powerful when it is a two-way bridge: experience flows from one generation to the next, while new ideas and perspectives flow back,” says Sudeendra Koushik, president of the IEEE Technology and Engineering Management Society and an ILC keynote speaker. “This approach transforms mentorship from simply passing on information into one where the next generation can question, experiment, innovate, and ultimately surpass what came before them.”Seasoned professionals should encourage independent, disruptive thinkers rather than carbon copies of themselves, Prasad says.“Legacy leadership is about building continuity,” she says. “We should not simply prepare the next generation to follow the paths we created; we should give them the confidence, knowledge, and networks to challenge those paths, create new ones, and take technology further than we imagined.”Designing your next chapterLeadership does not need to stop when one’s job ends; it can evolve. Seasoned, retired professionals can continue contributing meaningful service through pathways that align with their personal passions. They include:Advisory boards: steering corporate, technical, or community organizations.Civic engagement: applying engineering methodologies to solve community challenges.Volunteerism: mentoring the next generation of grassroots innovators through professional networks including IEEE.Those pathways offer experienced professionals an opportunity to redefine success, not in terms of position, authority, or personal achievement but in terms of sustained impact.“Retirement from a job should never mean retirement from purpose,” Koushik says. “Our experience becomes even more valuable when we use it in service of the profession, society, and the generation that follows.”At the same time, the collaborative continuum relies on a proactive younger generation. Emerging leaders need to take responsibility for building their professional connections, Prasad says, advising: “Be bold, stay curious, and build your network early!”A space for continuityThe conference is designed to combine a drive to cultivate emerging innovators with a deep reservoir of industry stewardship and strategic perspective. Rather than a single classroom session, the conference will feature a dedicated career-readiness and mentorship track where attendees can explore practical frameworks for building strategic professional networks, connecting with peer advocates, and establishing reciprocal knowledge-sharing opportunities across generations.By participating, seasoned professionals can ensure their decades of expertise continue to yield dividends for generations to come.“Our professional legacy is not the technology we build, the titles we earn, or the awards we receive,” Ranaweera says. “It is the knowledge we share, the lives we influence, and the future we help others create.”You can view the agenda, read speaker biographies, and secure your seat at the ILC online.

Entertainment.title: Lil Wayne Reveals New York Yankees Forced Redesign of Original Young Money Logo
Entertainment.text: SummaryLil Wayne revealed on 'The Joint Venture Show' podcast that the New York Yankees took legal action against the original Young Money logoThe MLB franchise issued a cease-and-desist letter claiming the stacked YM logo closely mirrored its interlocking NY emblemWayne respected the team's legacy and elected to change the logo rather than contest the legal noticeLil Wayne has revealed that the New York Yankees forced him to retire the original Young Money logo due to trademark concerns. Speaking alongside Craig Carton on The Joint Venture Show, the hip-hop icon detailed how a legal warning from the MLB franchise prompted an early visual redesign for his record label.While reflecting on his first Miami apartment at age 19—which featured a custom door displaying the initial stacked "YM" insignia—Wayne explained that the Yankees issued a formal cease-and-desist letter. The baseball team argued that the label's stacked typography appeared too similar to their iconic interlocking "NY" emblem, a design with roots tracing back to an 1877 NYPD Medal of Valor created by Tiffany & Co. before its adoption by the team in 1909. Wayne revealed, "They just sent me a cease and desist. And I had to stop using it... I just changed my logo."Rather than engaging in a legal dispute with the organization, Wayne chose to comply immediately and replace the logo. He shared, "I felt more cooler getting a letter from the Yankees." The rapper shared that he held no resentment toward the team, citing his respect for the franchise's legendary status and considering the cease-and-desist a memorable moment during his rise in the music industry.Listen to his story above.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Come Along With Me: Target by Design’s NYFW Party at New Museum
Entertainment.text: NYFW surely has no shortage of beautiful things behind glass cases or on the runway. But it’s times like these we often forget: some of the most carefully considered items are those we handle every day. Last week, Target took over NYC’s New Museum for Target by Design, an immersive two-day pop-up celebrating its love affair with everyday design and the creatives pushing it forward.The experience began straight out of the elevators, kicking off with a trip through Target’s archives. A kinetic archival installation spread throughout the first room, and I explored some of the brand’s most memorable products and collaborations through the years — from 2010 garments by Jean Paul Gaultier, to Michael Graves’ 90s homeware collection, and, of course, the iconic red shopping bag.For the occasion, Target handed over its classic tote to a collective of creative leaders, debuting designs by Public School, Daniel Arsham, Chloë Sevigny, Venus Williams, and more. With the artists’ touch, the humble shopping bag became everything from a sculpture, a statement piece, or an elevated basic.Guests could have a go at creating their own bags at a customization station nearby. Inspiration from KBB by Kahlana Barfield Brown and whimsy from Laila Gohar came through when it came time for my design. The details made it personal: a custom line-up of pins, print overlays, lanyards, and charms. I wanted the finished piece to feel personal and playful, with nods to the bag’s nostalgic heritage design.DJs SOFI TUKKER, Louise Chen, and Amrit Tietz carried the evening, while cocktails and bites made their way through the floor. The dance floor doubled as additional installations, turning the typical Target retail experience into surreal encounters, like a mirrored selfie room made up of self-checkout cameras, or another where Bullseye the Oracle read my shopping fortune.By night, the Target by Design crowd simmered back into the bustle of Fashion Week, bullseye totes slung over my shoulder. And while a classic is a classic for a reason, it’s nice to remember there’s always room for a little reinvention.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Dartio Vitale Joins Armani Group & Kai Cenat Makes NYFW Debut in This Week's Top Fashion News
Entertainment.text: SummaryNikeSKIMS targets Greater China with a Shanghai retail destination, while Parisian skate label VILLAGE PM officially enters the US market. Gap partners with A.P.C., Kith catalogs its footwear archive in a massive print volume, and Kai Cenat debuts his VIVET label at NYFW.Dario Vitale helms Emporio Armani and Giorgio Armani accessories.Dario Vitale Appointed Creative Director of Emporio Armani and Giorgio Armani AccessoriesThe Armani Group named Dario Vitale as the new creative director for Emporio Armani and Giorgio Armani Accessories. The move marks a significant generational transition, representing the first external design leader hired for a primary line since founder Giorgio Armani passed away in September 2025. Vitale takes over after spending 14 years shaping Miu Miu's ready-to-wear direction and a brief stint at Versace. He immediately steps into the dual role, preparing to debut his first runway collection for the Fall/Winter 2027 season, following Silvana Armani and Leo Dell’Orco’s final co-ed presentation on September 24.NikeSKIMS Expands Into China With Debut Apparel and Footwear CollectionNike and SKIMS are pushing their joint venture into Greater China. The NikeSKIMS China collection arrives September 29, offering a full system of performance apparel, footwear, and accessories. The launch merges Nike's Dri-FIT technology with SKIMS' signature sculpting fits across nine material fabrications, ranging from sheer layers to matte compression. Campaign visuals feature notable athletes like Chloe Kim and Stephanie Au. To support the regional rollout, the brands will open a dedicated physical pop-up at Shanghai’s HKRI Taikoo Hui, offering custom hemming and early access through February 2027.Kai Cenat Debuts Inaugural VIVET Collection During New York Fashion WeekDigital creator Kai Cenat presented his first clothing collection at New York Fashion Week for the Spring/Summer 2027 season. Hosted at Cipriani in Lower Manhattan on September 12, the VIVET runway show spanned three acts tracking his design education in Italy, shifting from raw hoodies to structured suiting. The brand emphasizes luxury leather goods, highlighted by the hero Cenova and Streamer bags, alongside heavyweight outerwear and treated denim. Cenat also wove subtle nods to his Haitian heritage and carnival traditions into specific garments. Select pieces from the debut are currently available online.Kith and Assouline Announce 'Kith: The Footwear Archive' Celebrating 15-Year HistoryIn recognition of its 15th anniversary, Kith partnered with luxury publisher Assouline to document founder Ronnie Fieg's footwear design history. The resulting 444-page book, Kith: The Footwear Archive, features photography by Tyler Mansour showcasing over 1,800 released models and unreleased developmental prototypes across major brand partnerships. Releasing September 30, the publication arrives in a Classic edition and a 300-unit Ultimate Edition signed by Fieg and housed in a monogrammed leather clamshell. Ahead of the drop, Kith is displaying all 1,800 pairs at a public exhibition in Brooklyn from September 25 to 27.VILLAGE PM Debuts the 2PM Silhouette, Marking Expansion Into the US for FW26Paris-based skate brand VILLAGE PM officially enters the US market for the FW26 season. Accompanying the expansion is the debut of the new 2PM sneaker. Founded last year by Basile Lapray and Bram De Cleen, the label applies high-performance climbing shoe mechanisms to progressive skate designs. The 2PM model evolves the brand's formula with a more structured, lower-to-the-ground profile while maintaining its signature asymmetrical fit and sticky rubber wrap. The brand’s US rollout spans a domestic webstore and premier retailers including MAXFIELD, Dover Street Market, and UNION.Gap and A.P.C. Announce Collaborative 37-Piece Apparel and Accessories CollectionGap and A.P.C. merged classic American sportswear with Parisian refinement for a 37-piece capsule collection releasing today. Ranging from $28 to $328 USD, the assortment highlights premium Japanese denim pieces, including men's relaxed jeans and women's sculptural jackets lined with archival graphics. The line goes beyond denim, incorporating tailored outerwear, cashmere knitwear, corduroy sets, and reworked hoodies sporting Gap's arch logo in A.P.C.'s signature typography. The drop hit retail channels this morning, backed by a Montmartre-shot campaign film featuring rapper ian and DJ Paloma Le Friant.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Glenn Martens Is Leaving Diesel
Entertainment.text: SummaryGlenn Martens is stepping down as Diesel’s Creative Director after his SS27 Milan show, ending a transformative six-year tenure.Martens will remain creative head of Maison Margiela under parent company OTB Group; no replacement for Diesel is announced yet.Glenn Martens’ six-year run as Creative Director of Italian denim label Diesel will conclude after his SS27 runway presentation, scheduled for September 22 at Milan Fashion Week. The news brings to a close a fruitful tenure from Martens, which injected the 1978-born brand with renewed vitality.Formerly known for Y/Project until 2024, Martens joined Diesel in 2020, updating the brand’s appeal for a new generation of shoppers with his cutting-edge aesthetic and inventive approach. Diesel founder and OTB Chairman Renzo Rosso said that Martens “brought Diesel back to the centre of the global fashion conversation while preserving the openness, energy and accessibility that have always distinguished us,” in an official statement. "We are deeply grateful for everything he has achieved," he continued.Announced by the Diesel owner this Friday, OTB Group was sure to note that Martens won't be leaving the conglomerate entirely, confirming that he would remain the creative head of Maison Margiela. Martens took up the highly-regarded role, formerly held by John Galliano, in 2025 and received consistent praise for his continued commitment to Margiela's creative ethos. As of the time of writing, Diesel has not announced an official replacement for Martens.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: ‘House of Kong’: An Illustrated History of Gorillaz
Entertainment.text: “If you want something done right, do it yourself.” Perhaps the saying ran through the minds of Damon Albarn and Jamie Hewlett in their shared London flat back in the ’90s. Blur frontman Albarn and Hewlett, the Tank Girl comic illustrator, had become bored with the era’s celebrity artifice, and sought to double down with a group — half art, half music — the industry had yet to witness. In came Gorillaz, the world’s first virtual band.25 years later, the Gorillaz universe keeps getting richer. On the occasion of their now ninth studio album, The Mountain, an immersive exhibition dedicated to the band’s misadventures has landed in New York City. House of Kong has settled into Brooklyn’s Agger Fish Building quite nicely, with a month-long run culminating in its Madison Square Garden show on September 29.Set inside Kong Studios — Gorillaz’ HQ on a sleepy Essex hilltop — the hour-long experience tours the history of artwork, music, artifacts, and mythology behind bassist Murdoc Niccals, singer 2D, drummer Russel Hobbs, and guitarist Noodle. We don’t want to give too much away (though if you’re looking for Lucian Freud’s Francis Bacon painting someone stole in 1988, 2D is a prime culprit). This is all to say, the lore runs deep. View this post on Instagram A post shared by HYPEBEAST (@hypebeast)Gorillaz has left a pretty serious footprint on culture, netting countless chart-toppers, hundreds of shows, awards, and a Guinness World Record. But music is only half the story. Beyond a starry coterie of collaborators and features, or a knack for genre-bending, Gorillaz has gone on to inspire a new generation of animators chasing that punkish rush that first put them on the map and the appetite for invention that kept them there.House of Kong is the first IRL experience dedicated to the band’s full visual legacy, and includes entire galleries of early concepts, scrapped characters, and unreleased videos through the years. The exhibition is less of a retrospective than “an installation that takes a glance backwards in order to identify the path ahead,” as creative director Stephen Gallagher, and both co-founders, made clear earlier this year. Even so, consider this our excuse to revisit the good ole (demon) days with an illustrated history of the Gorillaz’ many eras.Phase One: Celebrity Take Down (1998-2002)The OG Gorillaz character designs, off the bat, claimed roots in counterculture comics tradition. Thick lines, geometric shapes, exaggerated poses, rendered in bold, flat colors made for the cool, scrappy-and-sleek look that defined Gen 1. Hewlett, semi-fresh off his Tank Girl tenure, brought a similar soft rebellious charm to this new crew. The members seemed to represent their own rockstar archetypes. But the Gorillaz story, as we would soon see, was so much more.Highlights from this era: “Clint Eastwood,” going back to the basics, and Murdoc rejecting a 2001 Mercury Prize nomination, middle finger high, against the wishes of their then-label.Phase Two: Slowboat to Hades (2004-2008)The Demon Days era gave way to muted palettes and heavier textures, giving the characters more angular designs. The album itself bore a darker concept, circling themes of war and corruption, and the visuals tended to its sound: a denser, more hip-hop-driven project shaped by Danger Mouse, backed by the likes of MF DOOM, De La Soul, Shaun Ryder, and Dennis Hopper. The Gorillaz, unlike most animations, had already grown up.Highlights from this era: Jamie Hewlett’s limited-edition Stained Glass Windows prints featuring the members across five chapel-like panels, published by Hewlett and Banksy's now-defunct Pictures on Walls.Phase Three: Escape to Plastic Beach (2008-2013)The band ups the gloss for its third studio album, with a brighter, more summery palette to fit the psychedelic sound. In the project’s storyline, the band flees England for Plastic Beach, a remote island off the coast of Southern Chile to establish a new HQ. The island itself is made up of trash floating in the Pacific, congealed into one Pacific landmass. The residence up top, according to the fictional lore, was designed by M.C. Escher.Band portraits, here, are swapped for landscape pieces, gesturing towards the political concerns in the animated world, alongside Albarn and bassist Paul Simonon’s real-life involvement with Greenpeace in 2011. While a push towards CGI-like visuals took the band into new territory, it didn’t fare well with all fans. For the first time, the group’s fictional world started to feel too real, though it tested the waters for future 3D styles in later phases.Highlights from this era: A four-meter tall Plastic Beach model and the storyboard-turned-visualizer for an unrealized “Rhinestone Eyes” music video.Phase Four: We Are Still Humanz (2014-2018)After a seven-year hiatus, Humanz saw a return to Gorillaz’ 2D roots, but with a noticeably polished upgrade. Flatter character designs sit against richly detailed 3D backgrounds, while sharper lines and more refined proportions give the band a slicker, more mature look. Partly developed to better accommodate a tricky hologram set-up during their live shows, the style also showed that Gorillaz was always about reinventing itself, and not just running back its greatest hits, aesthetically speaking.Highlights from this era: The “Saturnz Barz (Spirit House)” music video, which also toured as a touring immersive experience, and the band’s first live-streamed Q&A on YouTube — a true feat in Gorillaz tech.Phase Five: No More Unicorns Anymore (2018-2019)With its more melancholic, stripped-back sound, The Now Now feels like a comedown from Humanz, with visuals following suit. With the rest of the band out of the picture, this project puts 2D, now a lone frontman, center stage. Album artwork features clean, few-toned graphic compositions with nods to ’80s retro-pop comic callbacks, making for one of the most distinct visual languages out of all the bodies of work.Highlights from this era: “Tranz” their first proper on-stage “live” performance, complete with trippy visuals by Hewlett and Nicos Livesey above a synth-rock number.Phase Six: Wish You Wear Ear (2019-2021)Song Machine, Season One: Strange Timez, released during COVID, had fans hyped. A culmination of the Song Machine project, an episodic web series of videos and singles, each were animated around the song’s featurees. From Slowthai, Elton John, and Robert Smith to Beck, St. Vincent, and ScHoolboy Q, the album’s sound reflected that of its Rolodex of guests and influences. The art, of course, was fittingly playful, hovering betweenp several aesthetics and illustrative designs.Highlights from this era: Can we say the whole series?Phase Seven: The Static Channel (2022-2024)Cracker Island takes place in Silver Lake, Los Angeles, after a sinkhole ousts the band from Kong once again. The concept, in part, reflected the real-life axing of Gorillaz’ Netflix feature, which would eventually turn into this album. Unpacking the cultish air around internet echo chambers and life online, the foursome is rendered in a more pristine 3D style, true to the album’s exploration of the contemporary soullessness and corporate-controlled culture that spurred the group’s formation in the first place. This go-around at 3D felt more true to Gorillaz’ progression and themes thus far, balancing comic stylization and hyperreal figuration.Highlights from this era: The “Cracker Island” music video, where 2D and Russel appear near-zombified (à la “Clint Eastwood”) beside Thundercat. The Gorillaz Art Book, the band’s first visual collaboration, was also released during this period. Alongside archival artwork from Hewlett, the 288-pager features more than several re-styled versions of Murdoc, 2D, Noodle, and Russel by 40 artists and musicians.Phase Eight: The Mountain (2025–)This brings us to The Mountain, arguably Gorillaz’ most visually intricate endeavor yet. With clear cues from India throughout, the album, released in February 2026, thematically dials in on death, grief, and the afterlife, inspired by profound personal loss experienced by both Albarn and Hewlett during its production. The two considered pain through a more “optimistic” attitude that Hindus, Buddhists, and Sikhs held around death. Unused vocals from former Gorillaz collaborators who have since passed were also repurposed, with Dennis Hopper, Mark E. Smith, and Bobby Womack making appearances on the project.The artwork is rich with visual references to Jaipur, known as the “Pink City,” where Hewlett had an unexpected two-month stay caring for his mother-in-law. Hand-drawn, anatomically detailed characters sit above ornate settings with deeper shading and shadows throughout. Spiritual discovery runs through the illustrations, too, with earthy palettes abound and warm, albeit curious, expressions fashioned on band members in key album imagery.Highlights from this era: “The Mountain, The Moon Cave and The Sad God” short film, created with The Line Studio, is entirely hand-drawn and made to emulate old-school animation techniques from the ’60s and ’70s.In an interview last year, Albarn, about the artistic and sonic cohesion, called The Mountain “the next record after Plastic Beach” alluding his and Hewlett’s separation through the 2010's. What we're gathering is that Gorillaz is hitting their stride once again. Even 25 years on, they’ve yet again carved another world to disappear into. Art & Culture.title: Yoshitomo Nara and Mark Rothko Lead Sotheby’s ‘PSYCHO’ Exhibition
Art & Culture.text: SummarySotheby’s PSYCHO explores identity, alienation and psychological tension through art and literature.Rothko and Yoshitomo Nara anchor the exhibition and upcoming auctions.The Hong Kong showcase runs through September 27, with sales on September 28–29.Sotheby’s Maison in Hong Kong is turning its latest biannual curated exhibition toward the more unsettled corners of the psyche with PSYCHO: Identity Alienation Shadow Duality. On view through September 27, the exhibition brings together museum-quality loans and works from Sotheby’s upcoming Modern & Contemporary Art auctions to examine how identity, obsession, fear, vanity and ambition surface through art and literature.Drawing on the psychological language of cinema and the written word, PSYCHO positions outward appearances against the tensions concealed beneath them, assembling works by Mark Rothko, Yoshitomo Nara, Tetsuya Ishida, Yayoi Kusama, Hans Bellmer, Lee Bul, Frank Auerbach, Paula Rego and more. Literary touchstones extend the premise beyond visual art, with first-edition copies of Bret Easton Ellis’ American Psycho and a 17th-century edition of Robert Burton’s The Anatomy of Melancholy further tracing themes of alienation, despair and fractured identity.Anchoring the exhibition and the September 28 Modern & Contemporary Evening Auction is Mark Rothko’s "Untitled (Plum and Dark Brown)" from 1964, a monumental two-meter canvas estimated to fetch between $78 million and $128 million HKD (approx. $9.9 million - $16.3 million USD). Created shortly before the artist’s Rothko Chapel series, its reduced plum-and-brown palette, restrained composition and enveloping scale reflect the increasingly introspective direction of Rothko’s late period, making it a fitting centerpiece for an exhibition concerned with what lies beneath apparently quiet surfaces.Yoshitomo Nara provides another major focal point with "The Crated Room in Iceland / Drawing Room," returning to public view after more than 15 years and making its auction debut with a $45 million to $65 million HKD estimate (approx. $5.7 million - $8.2 million USD). Created during Nara’s collaboration with graf, the installation surrounds viewers with a shipping-crate structure filled with 97 drawings, chairs, a CD player and personal objects, alongside a large-scale painting — effectively collapsing the distance between artwork, studio and the artist’s internal world.Elsewhere, PSYCHO expands its study of psychological and social unease through radically different visual languages. Tetsuya Ishida’s 1996 "Can’t Fly Anymore," estimated between $6 million and $8 million HKD (approx. $764k - $1 million USD), places his recurring everyman figure inside a rusting pirate-ship amusement ride, turning an image of attempted flight into a meditation on confinement, disillusionment and the uncertainty that followed Japan’s bubble-economy collapse. Lee Bul’s large-scale Heaven and Earth similarly draws personal and political trauma into a disorienting sculptural environment, combining a shattered tiled bathtub, black calligraphy ink and miniature mountain forms with references to Korea’s modern history. Together with works by Kusama, Alicja Kwade, David Altmejd and others, the exhibition frames psychological duality not as a singular condition but as something shaped by personal memory, social pressure, national history and perception.PSYCHO: Identity Alienation Shadow Duality remains on view at Sotheby’s Maison, LANDMARK CHATER, Hong Kong through September 27, while the Modern & Contemporary Evening Auction takes place September 28, followed by the Modern and Contemporary Day Auctions on September 29.
